demonstration.title: E1: account for all fourteen units

states.caption: The target contains fourteen exact units; the measuring stick contains six.
Place one six-unit copy against the target; eight target units are still uncovered.
A second six-unit copy fits. A third would exceed the target, so two units remain.

transitions.explanation: Create a copy of the six-unit stick; keep the original stick in its own row.

check.prompt: Could E1 use q = 1 and r = 8 for 14 divided by 6?
choices: No, because a remainder of 8 is not smaller than 6.
No, because remainders must always be zero.

simplerHelp.intro: Put fourteen counters in a row and use a tray that holds six.

steps.text: Move six counters into the first tray.
Move another six into a second tray. Two counters remain.

check.prompt: With 17 counters and trays of 5, how many counters remain after filling as many trays as possible?
check.explanation: Three trays use fifteen counters; two remain, and two is smaller than five.

simplerHelp.connection: The trays are copies of n, the original row is m, and the loose counters are the exact remainder r. Return to E1 and its two requirements.

demonstration.title: Smaller integers have only finitely many steps down

states.caption: Begin with divisor 6. Exactly five smaller positive integer values are available.
For 14 divided by 6, the remainder is 2. A continuing pass moves n from 6 to 2.
Now 6 divided by 2 leaves zero. E2 stops before zero could become a divisor.
The real-number track may continue 1/8, 1/16, …; none of those values is zero.

transitions.explanation: Apply one Euclid reduction; the real-number comparison independently halves once. These are two separately labeled processes.
Euclid encounters zero remainder and stops. The independent halving process remains positive.
Continue only the real-valued comparison. The formula proves all finite halving steps remain positive; the finite drawing alone would not.

check.prompt: What is missing from the claim “the value keeps getting smaller, so it must stop”?
choices: A guarantee that the decreasing value lies in a set such as the positive integers with no infinite strict descent.
A rule that the value decreases by exactly one.
check.explanation: Strict descent through positive integers suffices even when values are skipped. Arbitrary positive real values can decrease forever.

simplerHelp.intro: Use a numbered staircase rather than an unmarked ramp.

steps.text: Start at step 6. Count the smaller positive steps: 1 through 5.
Euclid can jump to 2, but every continuing jump must go to a smaller positive label.
On the separate ramp, 1, 1/2, 1/4, … stay positive forever. The integer labels are the important restriction.

check.prompt: A process starts at the positive integer 9 and strictly lowers it at every continuation. Can it continue forever?
choices: No, because only eight positive integers are below 9.
We must watch every possible run first.
check.explanation: Every continuation consumes another lower integer value; there are only finitely many below the start.

simplerHelp.connection: The staircase is the proof behind the original phrase “smaller positive integer.” It does not claim one fixed step bound for every input.

demonstration.title: Finite work can still be slow

states.caption: A finite integer instruction supplies finite data and ordinary operations.
Multiply four by 119 using a finite exact procedure; the product is 476.
Subtract 476 from 544. The exact result is 68.
Six observed zero digits cannot decide whether every later digit is zero.

objects.label: missing instruction
objects.value: How can a finite inspection settle all unseen digits?

transitions.explanation: Execute a finite multiplication. The separate decimal panel illustrates only finite prefix inspection, not the same input.
Finish the exact integer calculation. No uninspected portion remains in those finite integers.
Two different infinite decimals agree with every displayed digit. An instruction to read all digits would not finish.

check.prompt: Which claim follows from an operation taking a very long but finite time?
choices: It may still be effective; efficiency is a different question.
check.explanation: Effectiveness asks for an exact finite method per step. A long step may be effective, and infinitely many effective steps can still make a divergent run.

simplerHelp.intro: Compare a very long finite checklist with a checklist that literally never ends.

steps.text: You can in principle finish one million written items, although it may be slow.
“Read every digit” of an arbitrary infinite decimal never reaches a final item.
Even a short, finishable action can be repeated forever. Per-step work and whole-run termination are different.

check.prompt: A program adds 1 to a finite integer, then repeats forever. What is true?
choices: Its step is effective, but the run does not terminate.
Its run is finite because the instruction list is short.
check.explanation: Each addition finishes; the endless repetition prevents termination.

simplerHelp.connection: The finite checklist corresponds to effectiveness. Whether the program eventually enters an output state is the separate finiteness requirement.

demonstration.title: The same run has two different legitimate counts

states.caption: A permitted pair is an input, before any application of f.
Initialization adds a placeholder remainder and selects E1.
E1 assigns the exact remainder 2 and selects E2.
E2 sees a positive remainder and changes only the phase to 3.
E3 carries the old divisor and remainder into the next pair.
E1 computes the zero remainder and selects E2.
E2 returns the singleton output (2). This is its first occurrence.

transitions.explanation: This is one application of f: a pair becomes a phase-1 quadruple.
Keep m,n fixed; assign 14 mod 6 = 2 and phase 2.
Keep all data registers fixed; change only the phase.
The single formal transition maps (m,n,p,3) to (n,p,p,1).
Keep m = 6 and n = 2; assign 6 mod 2 = 0 and phase 2.
The zero branch maps the working state to the output (2).

check.prompt: For this displayed formal run, what do “2” and “6” count?
choices: 2 is the number of remainder divisions; 6 is the number of applications of f.
2 is the input size; 6 is the output.
2 and 6 are conflicting measurements of the same specified operation.
check.explanation: E1 runs twice. The formal model also counts initialization, E2 tests, and E3 reduction, producing six transitions.

simplerHelp.intro: Keep two tally sheets beside the same 14,6 calculation.

steps.text: Add a mark to the division sheet only when a remainder is computed.
Add a mark to the transition sheet every time the complete formal state changes according to f.
At output 2, the sheets read two divisions and six transitions. Both counts are right because they count different operations.

check.prompt: If a program takes 15 transitions, does that by itself prove no faster program could solve the problem?
choices: No; that measurement concerns one program and one cost model.
check.explanation: A measurement does not prove an impossibility result about all possible procedures.

simplerHelp.connection: Return to the original distinction: analysis measures specified resources; a theory claim about existence or limits requires a separate argument.

demonstration.observerConvention: The transition counter and division tally are annotations outside the machine state. They are not coordinates of Q.

demonstration.title: One parcel, one instruction, one next state

states.caption: Start at A: parcel left, instruction CHECK. The other five cards show all the remaining allowed states.
Apply f to A. CHECK changes only the instruction to MOVE; the parcel stays left.
Apply f to B. MOVE carries the same parcel right and selects CHECK.
Apply f to C. CHECK sees the parcel on the right and selects DONE. E is an output.
Apply f once more for inspection: E remains exactly E. There is no additional work after the first output.
Select the gallery card D. This is a comparison, not a continuation of the preceding run; D is unreachable from the allowed starts.
Apply f to the selected D. MOVE leaves the already-right parcel right and selects CHECK, so f(D) = C.
Select Z. HOLD fixes this full state, but Z is not in Ω. Being unchanged is not by itself being finished.

transitions.explanation: Apply f(A) = B. Identical parcel positions can belong to different states because the instruction matters.
Apply f(B) = C. Preserve the parcel object’s identity as its location changes.
Apply f(C) = E. Output membership, not lack of movement, determines completion.
Apply f(E) = E. Every coordinate of the machine state stays unchanged.
Navigation selects D to inspect totality; this is not an application of f and must not increment a machine transition counter.
Totality supplies f(D) even though D is not reached from I = {A,E}.
Select the non-output fixed point Z to test the converse of the fixed-output condition. The displayed table gives f(Z) = Z.

check.prompt: If a run starts at E, which is in both I and Ω, how many transitions are needed to finish?
choices: One, because every run must call f at least once.
It cannot start there because I and Ω must be disjoint.
check.explanation: The definition permits overlap. The initial state already belongs to Ω, so its first-hit time is zero.

simplerHelp.intro: A state is one complete snapshot: where the parcel is and what instruction happens next.

steps.text: A and B both put the parcel on the left. A says CHECK; B says MOVE. Those are different snapshots.
From B, move the parcel right and change the badge to CHECK. The result is C.
The card E belongs to the output set. If E is the starting card, nothing needs to happen.
The card Z never changes, but it has no output membership. It is a trap, not a completed delivery.

check.prompt: A card says “parcel left, MOVE.” Which next card does this model prescribe?
check.explanation: The complete table says f(B) = C: MOVE carries the parcel right and selects CHECK.

simplerHelp.connection: The six allowed cards are Q, the marked starting cards are I, the marked finished card is Ω, and the table gives f for every card. The gallery and viewer controls are not part of the parcel’s state.

demonstration.title: A finite prefix and a proof of an infinite run

states.caption: Compare two separately defined methods. Their outputs use the distinct marker DONE.
After one transition in each method, the countdown is 1 and the increasing method is 1.
After two transitions, countdown zero is still not the output marker DONE.
The countdown first reaches DONE after three transitions. The increasing method is at 3.
Every state of the increasing run is an integer k. DONE is not an integer, so that run never enters its output set.

objects.label: finite observation
objects.value: Seeing only 0,1,2,3 is not the proof. The formula for every k is.

transitions.explanation: Apply the countdown rule once and the separately defined increasing rule once.
The numeral zero and the output marker DONE are different states.
The countdown maps zero to DONE and finishes. The increasing method applies another increment.
This is a proof explanation, not another transition. Establish x_0 = 0 and x_(k+1) = x_k + 1 = k + 1.

check.prompt: A simulator shows ten transitions without an output. What does that fact alone establish?
choices: There was no output among the observed states.
The next transition must be an output.
check.explanation: A bounded observation establishes only what happened within that prefix. A separate invariant, cycle argument, or other proof is needed to establish divergence.

simplerHelp.intro: Write each complete snapshot on a card and put a number above each arrow.

steps.text: The initial card is x₀. No arrow has been crossed yet.
For the countdown, cross arrows 2 → 1 → 0 → DONE. The first output is reached after three arrows.
For the increasing rule, each card is another integer. A separate DONE card can never appear because the rule only adds one.

check.prompt: If the initial card itself says DONE, what is its first-hit time?
check.explanation: An output present at x₀ requires no transition.

simplerHelp.connection: The cards are states and the arrows are applications of f. Navigation frames are not the mathematical clock.

demonstration.title: Read the phase badge before acting

states.caption: A permitted pair is an input, before any application of f.
Initialization adds a placeholder remainder and selects E1.
E1 assigns the exact remainder 2 and selects E2.
E2 sees a positive remainder and changes only the phase to 3.
E3 carries the old divisor and remainder into the next pair.
E1 computes the zero remainder and selects E2.
E2 returns the singleton output (2). This is its first occurrence.
For completeness, f maps the output (2) to itself. The first-hit time remains six.

transitions.explanation: This is one application of f: a pair becomes a phase-1 quadruple.
Keep m,n fixed; assign 14 mod 6 = 2 and phase 2.
Keep all data registers fixed; change only the phase.

Keep m = 6 and n = 2; assign 6 mod 2 = 0 and phase 2.
The zero branch maps the working state to the output (2).
This formal self-loop does not delay termination: the run already finished at its first output.

check.prompt: From (14,6,2,2), what is the next complete state?

steps.text: Phase 1 means calculate the remainder and change the badge to 2.

check.prompt: What does (6,2,0,2) do next?

simplerHelp.connection: The circled pair is θ₀, the replacement is φ₀, and the unchanged tiles form the prefix α and suffix ω. The instruction badge records the branch destination.

demonstration.terminationArgument: Each ab → ba exchange reduces by exactly one the finite number of ordered position pairs with an a before a b. Other pair relationships are unchanged. That nonnegative integer cannot decrease forever.

emptyPatternSupplement.intro: The empty word ε is a permitted pattern. Its leftmost occurrence is the boundary before the first tile.
emptyPatternSupplement.example: For σ = ba and φ = a, replacing the leftmost ε inserts a at the beginning: ba → aba. The existing b and a tiles shift right without changing order.

check.prompt: Where is the leftmost occurrence of the empty pattern?
choices: Nowhere, because it has no letters.
check.explanation: The shortest possible prefix is ε, so the chosen boundary is the start. For an empty input word, that same boundary is also its end.

steps.text: You can complete that tiny action exactly.
After it, both the tile and the instruction card are identical to their starting state.
Nothing can change on later visits, so an output card will never be reached.
With no tile, the specified missing-pattern branch can instead lead straight to the output card.

check.prompt: Which fact proves the a-input loops?
choices: The same full non-output state repeats under the same deterministic rule.
check.explanation: The current state determines every successor. Repeating the full state outside Ω therefore repeats the same future indefinitely.

simplerHelp.connection: Effectiveness explains why each action can be carried out. Finiteness asks whether every permitted run reaches Ω. The two obligations must be checked separately.
